title: The SNAP Trial: 2-Year Results of a Double-Blind Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial of a Silicon Nitride Versus a PEEK Cage in Patients After Lumbar Fusion Surgery
condition_or_topic: Lumbar interbody fusion for chronic low back pain, comparing Si3N4 and PEEK cages.
clinical_background: Interbody cages help stabilize the spine, restore alignment, preserve disc and foraminal height, and support bone fusion. PEEK is widely used and has yielded high fusion rates and favorable clinical outcomes, but its hydrophobic surface may impede direct bone attachment. Si3N4 is a ceramic alternative whose reported properties include bone integration, reduced CT and MRI artifacts, and lower bacterial activity than PEEK and Ti. An animal study reported similar mechanical stability and bone formation with Si3N4 and PEEK cages, while a cervical fusion trial found no statistically significant differences in clinical outcomes or fusion rates. When SNAP was designed, clinical trial evidence for Si3N4 cages in the lumbar spine had not yet been published.
objectives: To determine whether lumbar fusion with a Si3N4 cage produces clinical improvement comparable to a PEEK cage, using RMDQ at 12 months as the primary non-inferiority comparison.
To compare clinical and radiological outcomes after lumbar fusion with Si3N4 versus PEEK cages through 2 years.
clinical_question: In patients undergoing lumbar fusion for chronic low back pain with or without leg pain, does a Si3N4 cage, compared with a PEEK cage, provide non-inferior improvement in RMDQ at 12 months, and how do clinical and radiological outcomes compare through 2 years?
interpretation: Both cage groups improved in disability and pain over 24 months, and their fusion outcomes were comparable. Nevertheless, the findings do not provide sufficient evidence that Si3N4 is non-inferior to PEEK under the prespecified RMDQ margin of 2.6 points. Operative time and blood loss were significantly greater with Si3N4. Complications and revisions were more frequent in that group, but those differences were not statistically significant. The authors relate the longer operative time partly to more 2-level procedures and to replacement of 2 Si3N4 cages that fractured during insertion; a Si3N4-group blood-loss value of 1700ml also skewed the blood-loss comparison.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The RMDQ improvements and fusion results were consistent with those reported in other spinal fusion studies. Secondary outcomes were also comparable with published PEEK results of 24 to 36 for VAS back pain, 26 to 42 for VAS leg pain and 9 to 20 for ODI. The authors cite Stratford et al for the observation that a clinically important RMDQ change varies with the initial score; because the initial score in this trial was 14, they note that a higher non-inferiority margin could have been considered, while cautioning that the margin cannot be determined solely from an individual patient's minimum detectable difference.
clinical_implications: The observed similarity in clinical and radiological outcomes does not establish non-inferiority of Si3N4 to PEEK at the prespecified RMDQ margin.
A fusion judged inadequate technically or radiographically does not necessarily imply an unsuccessful clinical outcome, since vertebral stability may precede visible radiographic fusion.
limitations: Using a single oblique cage to improve the accuracy of CT fusion measurements may have influenced the results because it is mechanically less stable than 2 parallel cages; the authors suggest this may also help explain the revision rate of 15.2%.
The non-inferiority conclusion depends on the prespecified RMDQ margin of 2.6 points, for which other choices might have been possible.
Amedica Corporation, the manufacturer of the Si3N4 cage, funded the study, creating a potential source of bias that the authors sought to minimize.
Because PEEK cages are radiolucent, the implant–bone interface could not be assessed reliably and was excluded from the radiological analyses.
strengths: To reduce potential bias, an independent Clinical Research Organization participated in study management, an independent organization performed the statistical analyses, and a separate independent unit conducted radiographic measurements.
open_questions: The authors state that a clear relationship between radiographic bony fusion and a good clinical outcome has not been established.
future_directions: Future studies should consider stratifying patients by their initial RMDQ scores when assessing clinically relevant changes.
study_design: Multicenter randomized controlled trial designed to assess non-inferiority, with patients and clinical observers blinded. Participants were assigned using a centralized 24-hour online computerized randomization system.

population.description: Patients with chronic low-back pain, with or without leg pain, undergoing single- or double-level instrumented lumbar fusion. Between 2012 and 2015, 100 patients were enrolled at 2 centers; 8 were subsequently excluded because of protocol violations or cancellation of surgery, leaving 92 randomized patients.
inclusion_criteria: Male or female patients aged 18-75 years.
Chronic low-back pain that had not responded to at least 6 months of conservative care.
Disc degeneration of Pfirrmann Grade III or greater documented by MRI and standing x-ray.
Degeneration and/or degenerative or isthmic spondylolisthesis of Grade I or II.
exclusion_criteria: Previous failed fusion at the same level.
Degenerative spondylolisthesis greater than Grade II.
Alcoholism involving more than 5 units per day.
Active infection or previous infection at the surgical site.
Language skills insufficient to complete the questionnaires.
More than 2 symptomatic levels requiring fusion.
Planned emigration abroad in the year after inclusion.

interventions: Single- or double-level transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) with pedicle screw fixation and a single oblique Si3N4 cage (Valeo®OL), packed with locally harvested autograft.
comparators: Single- or double-level transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) with pedicle screw fixation and a single oblique PEEK cage (Phantom™PLIF), packed with locally harvested autograft.

primary: Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ) score on a 0-24 scale; the primary comparison between Si3N4 and PEEK was at 12 months, with a non-inferiority margin of 2.6 points.
secondary: Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) score on a 0-50 scale.
VAS scores for leg and back pain on a 0 to 100mm scale.
Patient- and surgeon-rated recovery on 7-point Likert scales; complete or almost complete recovery counted as a good outcome.
Radiological assessment of bony bridging on CT at 12 months, disc height and segmental alignment on radiographs, and the device-bone interface on CT at 12 months.
Subsidence, defined as a loss of >1mm in average disc height.
Segmental angular and translational motion on flexion/extension radiographs at 24 months; fusion was defined by angular motion <2 and translational motion < 0.5mm.

statistical_methods: The primary analysis used a mixed-effects model for repeated measurements (MMRM), with cage type and center as factors, baseline RMDQ as a fixed-effect covariate, patient as a random effect, an unstructured within-patient covariance matrix, and restricted maximum likelihood estimation. Missing values were not imputed for this analysis. The 12-month contrast estimated the mean RMDQ difference as Si3N4-PEEK with a one-sided confidence interval at a significance level of 2.5%; non-inferiority required its upper bound not to exceed 2.6 points. Assuming a standard deviation of 4 points, 50 patients per arm provided 90% power. A sensitivity analysis used Last Observation Carried Forward (LOCF) imputation followed by the same MMRM specification. Secondary continuous outcomes were analyzed with that MMRM specification; dichotomized patient and surgeon Likert outcomes were compared using Z-tests for proportions. Perioperative continuous variables were compared using two-sample t-tests and perioperative complication proportions using two-sample Z-tests, with two-sided p values.
follow_up: Measurements were scheduled before surgery and at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months; planned follow-up extended to 24 months.

secondary_results: Between 2012 and 2015, 100 patients entered the study at 2 centers (49 and 51). After 8 exclusions, 92 patients were randomized: PEEK 48 and Si3N4 44, with 46 per each center. At 24 months, 7 patients were lost to follow-up (7.6% drop-out rate).

At baseline, PEEK and Si3N4, respectively, had mean age (sd) 53.3 (9.2) and 55.4 (11.5); female patients 33 (68.8) and 28 (63.6); mean BMI (sd) 27.1 (4.3) and 27.1 (5.1); and smokers 31 (64.6) and 32 (72.7). Mean duration of complaints (sd) was 10.6 (9.3) for PEEK and 8.9 (6.1) for Si3N4.
Baseline complaint categories for PEEK and Si3N4, respectively, were radicular pain 8 (16.7) and 9 (20.5), combined back/radicular pain 39 (81.2) and 30 (68.2), and back pain 1 (2.1) and 5 (11.4).

Baseline diagnoses for PEEK and Si3N4, respectively, were degenerative disc disease 10 (20.8) and 13 (29.5); isthmic spondylolisthesis grade 1, 12 (25.0) and 11 (25.0); isthmic spondylolisthesis grade 2, 5 (10.4) and 6 (13.6); degenerative spondylolisthesis grade 1, 20 (41.7) and 14 (31.8); and degenerative spondylolisthesis grade 2, 1 (2.1) and 0 (0.0).

Operated levels for PEEK and Si3N4, respectively, were 1-level L3-L4, 4 (8.5) and 5 (11.4); L4-L5, 15 (31.9) and 11 (25.0); L5-S1, 21 (44.7) and 19 (43.2); L5-L6, 1 (2.1) and 0 (0.0); and L6-S1, 1 (2.1) and 1 (2.3). For 2-level procedures, L3-L5 accounted for 2 (4.3) and 1 (2.3); L4-L6, 0 (0.0) and 1 (2.3); L4-S1, 3 (6.3) and 5 (11.4); and L5-L6-S1, 0 (0.0) and 1 (2.3). The article also reports 5 PEEK patients and 8 Si3N4 patients receiving 2-level fusion.

Baseline mean (sd) scores for PEEK and Si3N4, respectively, were RMDQ 14.2 (4.3) and 14.8 (4.3); ODI 23.1 (7.4) and 22.5 (7.0); VAS leg 60.9 (20.7) and 58.9 (27.8); VAS back 62.3 (22.3) and 61.7 (21.9); and SF-36 Physical Functioning 37.0 (19.5) and 39.9 (19.4).

ODI mean (sd), PEEK versus Si3N4: at 3 months, 14.8 (9.4) versus 15.7 (8.0), p = 0.47; at 6 months, 10.7 (10.3) versus 12.3 (8.7), p = 0.49; at 12 months, 10.2 (10.2) versus 9.7 (9.1), p = 0.17; and at 24 months, 11.9 (10.3) versus 11.2 (10.9), p = 0.40. None of these between-group differences was statistically significant; the table identifies the p values as one-sided model estimates.

VAS leg mean (sd), PEEK versus Si3N4: at 3 months, 26.5 (27.7) versus 26.4 (26.2), p = 0.49; at 6 months, 23.6 (29.2) versus 26.2 (28.8), p = 0.47; at 12 months, 24.6 (28.4) versus 26.5 (22.9), p = 0.28; and at 24 months, 26.3 (25.3) versus 30.0 (31.3), p = 0.31. The reported between-group differences were not statistically significant; the p values are one-sided model estimates.

VAS back mean (sd), PEEK versus Si3N4: at 3 months, 34.9 (18.1) versus 37.9 (22.3), p = 0.49; at 6 months, 28.9 (23.3) versus 26.4 (25.4), p = 0.27; at 12 months, 30.2 (21.9) versus 31.0 (22.9), p = 0.39; and at 24 months, 34.8 (24.7) versus 38.2 (25.7), p = 0.45. The reported between-group differences were not statistically significant; the p values are one-sided model estimates.

SF36 physical functioning mean (sd), PEEK versus Si3N4: at 3 months, 59.2 (20.6) versus 58.0 (17.2), p = 0.44; at 6 months, 66.0 (23.9) versus 61.2 (19.7), p = 0.25; at 12 months, 73.1 (23.1) versus 68.5 (21.2), p = 0.24; and at 24 months, 71.5 (24.6) versus 64.9 (23.0), p = 0.20. The reported between-group differences were not statistically significant; the p values are one-sided model estimates.

Surgeon-perceived good recovery on the Likert scale, PEEK versus Si3N4: at 3 months, 73.3% versus 58.1%, p = 0.20; at 6 months, 76.2% versus 61.0%, p = 0.20; at 12 months, 78.6% versus 61.9%, p = 0.15; and at 24 months, 78.0% versus 56.3%, p = 0.08. Recovery was numerically higher with PEEK at each visit, but the differences were not statistically significant.

Patient-perceived good recovery on the Likert scale, PEEK versus Si3N4: at 3 months, 64.3% versus 58.1%, p = 0.72; at 6 months, 76.2% versus 56.1%, p = 0.09; at 12 months, 78.6% versus 64.3%, p = 0.23; and at 24 months, 75.0% versus 50.0%, p = 0.05. The authors describe the between-group recovery differences as not reaching statistical significance.

Mean disc height, PEEK versus Si3N4: postoperatively, 8.3 mm versus 8.1 mm, p = 0.63; at 3 months, 7.3 mm versus 7.3 mm, p = 0.91; at 6 months, 7.2 mm versus 7.0 mm, p = 0.67; at 12 months, 7.1 mm versus 6.9 mm, p = 0.67; and at 24 months, 7.1 mm versus 6.9 mm, p = 0.68. The reported between-group differences were not statistically significant; the p values are one-sided model estimates.

At 24 months, translational motion was 0.12 mm with PEEK and 0.14 mm with Si3N4 (two-sided p = 0.70); angular motion was 0.94 with PEEK and 1.18 with Si3N4 (two-sided p = 0.24). Neither between-group difference was statistically significant.
On the 24-month flexion/extension assessment, fusion rates were 88% for PEEK and 82% for Si3N4 (p = 0.40), without a statistically significant between-group difference.

CT at 12 months showed bony bridging in 42% of PEEK patients and 57% of Si3N4 patients (p = 0.13); the between-group difference was not statistically significant. The device-bone interface could not be assessed reliably for the radiolucent PEEK cages and was not included in the analyses.

main_conclusion: Both cage groups improved clinically, but the evidence was insufficient to establish that Si3N4 was non-inferior to PEEK. Si3N4 was associated with significantly greater operative time and blood loss; complications and revisions appeared more frequent with Si3N4, although those differences were not statistically significant.
narrative_summary:
The SNAP trial compared Si3N4 and PEEK cages for instrumented lumbar interbody fusion in a double-blind, multicenter, randomized non-inferiority study. Among 92 randomized patients, 48 received PEEK and 44 received Si3N4. Disability on the RMDQ was the primary outcome; the prespecified non-inferiority margin was 2.6 points for the comparison at 12 months. Clinical and radiographic assessments continued through 24 months.

Both groups improved on the RMDQ by up to 5-8 points, without statistically significant between-group differences in the reported clinical outcomes. Nevertheless, the confidence-interval boundary exceeded the 2.6-point margin, so the authors found insufficient evidence to conclude that Si3N4 was non-inferior. Fusion assessed by flexion/extension motion was 88% with PEEK versus 82% with Si3N4 (p = 0.40); CT showed bony bridging at 12 months in 42% versus 57%, respectively (p = 0.13).

Mean operative time was 127 (46) min with PEEK and 150 (51) min with Si3N4 (p = 0.03); mean blood loss was 317 (150) ml and 473 (332) ml, respectively (p = 0.01). By 24 months, revisions affected 4 out of 48 PEEK recipients (8.3%) and 10 out of 44 Si3N4 recipients (22.7%; p = 0.10). The authors also noted that their single-cage approach and chosen non-inferiority margin could affect interpretation.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Study design: This was a randomized controlled trial. Objective: The investigators compared Si3N4 and PEEK cages for lumbar interbody fusion, a procedure intended to stabilize vertebrae, restore alignment, and preserve disc and foraminal height. PEEK was commonly used, whereas Si3N4 offered osteointegrative properties. Methods: The multicenter, double-blind, non-inferiority trial enrolled patients with chronic low-back pain, with or without leg pain, who underwent single- or double-level instrumented TLIF with an oblique cage. The primary measure was RMDQ, with a non-inferiority margin of 2.6 points on its 24-point scale. Secondary measures covered ODI, VAS, SF-36 Physical Function, patient and surgeon Likert ratings, subsidence, segmental motion, and fusion. Follow-up was planned at 3, 6, 12, and 24-months. Results: Of 92 randomized patients, 48 received PEEK and 44 received Si3N4. Both groups improved by up to 5-8 RMDQ points. Clinical and radiographic outcomes did not differ significantly. Operative time and blood loss were significantly greater with Si3N4; complications and revisions were more frequent with Si3N4, but those differences were not statistically significant. Conclusion: The evidence was insufficient to establish non-inferiority of Si3N4 to PEEK.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Intervertebral fusion is used for chronic low-back pain, and both mechanical and biological conditions affect bone union. Earlier stand-alone bone grafts carried risks of nonunion, collapse, and donor-site morbidity. Interbody cages can support fusion while restoring alignment and maintaining disc and foraminal height. PEEK is widely used and has been associated with high fusion rates and favorable clinical results, but its hydrophobic surface can impede direct bone apposition and permit a fibrous layer around the implant. Ti surfaces may be more osteoinductive than PEEK, yet they cause CT and MRI artifacts and have been associated with greater subsidence risk. Approaches combining these materials, including Ti-coated endplates on PEEK cages and hydroxyapatite-coated PEEK cages, can improve osteointegration; reported clinical outcomes and fusion rates have not differed between these materials. Si3N4 is a strong, tough non-oxide ceramic that reduces CT and MRI scatter and artifacts. Its surface chemistry permits lower bacterial activity than PEEK and Ti. It received CE Mark and FDA market clearance as an interbody cage in 2008, and its mechanical, chemical, and osteoconductive properties have been described previously. An animal study reported similar mechanical stability and bone formation with Si3N4 and PEEK cages. An RCT of cages used after ACDF found no statistically significant difference in clinical outcomes or fusion rates between those materials. When SNAP was designed, lumbar clinical trial data for Si3N4 had not been published. The trial therefore compared the cages after lumbar fusion, primarily asking whether Si3N4 produced clinical improvement similar to PEEK; this article presents outcomes at 2 years.

document_sections.heading: Materials and Methods Study Design
document_sections.content: The study enrolled 100 patients with chronic low-back pain, with or without leg pain, for treatment using PEEK or Si3N4. It was designed as a multicenter, non-inferiority RCT that blinded patients and clinical observers. A previously published protocol described the study in greater detail. A centralized, continuously available computerized system assigned treatment. Table 1 sets out eligibility: inclusion required age 18-75 years, low-back pain persisting despite at least 6 months of conservative care, MRI and standing x-ray evidence of Pfirrmann Grade III or greater degeneration, degeneration and/or degenerative or isthmic spondylolisthesis of Grade I or II, and signed consent. Exclusions included osteoporosis, failed prior fusion at the same level, degenerative scoliosis, degenerative spondylolisthesis above Grade II, pregnancy, psychiatric or mental disease, alcohol intake of more than 5 units per day, active or previous surgical-site infection, active cancer, inability to complete questionnaires because of language skills, another study enrollment, more than 2 symptomatic levels requiring fusion, and planned emigration during the year after enrollment. Assessments took place before surgery and at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months.

document_sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
document_sections.content: The investigators conducted the study under the Declaration of Helsinki. A local medical ethics committee approved the protocol under NL34808.100.10, and every participant provided written informed consent.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Procedure
document_sections.content: Surgeons performed single- or double-level TLIF with pedicle screw fixation and one oblique PEEK or Si3N4 cage, identified respectively as Phantom™PLIF and Valeo®OL. The Si3N4 cage had 0 lordosis, compared with 6 for the PEEK implant. After exposure and pedicle screw placement, surgeons performed facetectomy and decompression on the symptomatic side, removed disc material, and prepared the endplates. They filled the cage with locally harvested autograft, inserted it into the disc space, and secured the screws and rods under compression. Patients began mobilizing on the first postoperative day without a brace. Figure 2 illustrates bone bridging between endplates after L4-L5 fusion with either cage at 24-months.

document_sections.heading: Clinical assessment.
document_sections.content: RMDQ, scored on a 0-24 scale, was the primary clinical measure. Secondary measures were SF-36, ODI on a 0-50 scale, leg- and back-pain VAS on a 0 to 100mm scale, and patient and surgeon recovery ratings on a 7-point Likert scale. Complete or almost complete recovery counted as a good Likert outcome. A neurological examination was conducted at each follow-up.

document_sections.heading: Radiological assessment.
document_sections.content: Fusion assessment followed criteria described by Burkus et al. It incorporated CT evidence of bridging bone at 12-months, changes in disc height and segmental alignment on lateral radiographs during follow-up, and CT assessment of the implant–bone interface at 12-months. Standing AP and lateral radiographs were obtained at 3, 6, 12, and 24-months; CT used 3.0mm slices. Average disc height was the mean of anterior and posterior measurements, and subsidence meant a decrease of >1mm in that average. Standing lateral flexion/extension images at 24-months assessed motion. Fusion required angular motion <2 and translational motion < 0.5mm. Each operated level was assessed separately in double-level procedures. An independent radiology organization performed the image analyses.

document_sections.heading: Primary efficacy analysis.
document_sections.content: The primary comparison tested Si3N4 non-inferiority to PEEK on RMDQ at 12 months, using a prespecified between-arm margin of 2.6 points. An MMRM included cage type and center as factors, baseline RMDQ as a fixed-effect covariate, and patient as a random effect. The analysis assumed an unstructured within-patient covariance matrix, used restricted maximum likelihood estimation, and did not impute missing observations. The 12-month contrast was the estimated mean RMDQ difference, Si3N4-PEEK, with a one-sided confidence interval at a 2.5% significance level. Non-inferiority required its upper boundary not to exceed 2.6 points. With an assumed standard deviation of 4 points, 50 patients per arm would provide 90% power.

document_sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis.
document_sections.content: To examine the effect of withdrawals, investigators repeated the primary MMRM specification after filling missing observations by Last Observation Carried Forward (LOCF).

document_sections.heading: Secondary efficacy analyses.
document_sections.content: At each visit, ODI, leg and back VAS, SF36, and radiological measurements were assessed using an MMRM with the same terms as the primary analysis. Dichotomized patient and surgeon Likert outcomes were compared by proportion Z-tests. Analyses used RStudio and nlme; plots used R base plotting functions and ggplot2.

document_sections.heading: Results Baseline Characteristics
document_sections.content: Between 2012 and 2015, 2 centers enrolled 100 patients, contributing 49 and 51 respectively. Eight were subsequently excluded because of protocol violations—including absent preoperative randomization, osteoporosis established after enrollment, or age at surgery—or because they canceled surgery after enrollment. The remaining 92 comprised 46 from each center; 48 were randomized to PEEK and 44 to Si3N4. Double-level fusion was performed in 5 PEEK patients and 8 Si3N4 patients. Table 2 presents demographic, diagnostic, operated-level, and baseline outcome characteristics. By 24 months, 7 patients had been lost to follow-up, a 7.6% drop-out rate.

document_sections.heading: Perioperative Results
document_sections.content: Table 3 reports operative characteristics and perioperative complications. Hospital stay did not differ between groups. Operative time was significantly higher with Si3N4, with a reported range of 72-290min versus 75-240min for PEEK; blood loss was also significantly higher, with ranges of 120-1700ml versus 100-700ml, respectively. Perioperative complications were somewhat more frequent in the Si3N4 group, without a statistically significant between-group difference.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Outcome
document_sections.content: RMDQ improved in both groups throughout 24-months of follow-up. PEEK patients had better RMDQ outcomes than Si3N4 patients at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months, but none of those differences was statistically significant. The prespecified 2.6-point non-inferiority criterion was not met: the upper confidence-interval boundary exceeded 2.6 at every follow-up. Table 4 presents clinical and radiographic outcomes over time. Leg- and back-pain VAS, SF36, and ODI showed improvement without significant between-group differences. Surgeons and patients generally rated recovery more favorably after PEEK at each follow-up, but those differences were not statistically significant.

document_sections.heading: Radiological Outcomes
document_sections.content: Table 4 also provides radiographic measurements. Mean disc height did not differ significantly between groups. Fusion based on flexion/extension angular or translational motion was 88% with PEEK versus 82% with Si3N4 (p = 0.40), without a significant difference. CT at 12 months showed bridging bone in 42% of PEEK patients versus 57% of Si3N4 patients (p = 0.13). Figure 5 depicts bridging bone around a Si3N4 cage at 12 months without visible lucency at its bone interface. Because PEEK cages were radiolucent, their interface with the endplates could not be assessed adequately; implant-interface lucency or osseous integration was therefore excluded from the analysis as unreliable. Over 24 months, 14 patients underwent revision, yielding a 15.2% revision rate. Table 5 describes the procedures. Revision affected 4 out of 48 PEEK patients (8.3%) and 10 out of 44 Si3N4 patients (22.7%); the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.10). Adjacent-level problems accounted for 5 out of 14 revisions.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The investigators interpreted disability, pain, and fusion outcomes as broadly comparable between cage groups. RMDQ improvement was consistent with other spinal-fusion studies and indicated favorable clinical outcomes at 2 years in both groups. Secondary scores were also consistent with previously reported PEEK results: VAS back pain of 24 to 36, VAS leg pain of 26 to 42, and ODI of 9 to 20. Observed fusion results likewise resembled published values.

document_sections.heading: Primary Outcome
document_sections.content: The trial hypothesized Si3N4 non-inferiority to PEEK using a 2.6-point RMDQ margin at 12-months. Although both groups improved by up to 5-8 points, the evidence did not establish non-inferiority. This judgment depends on the prespecified 2.6-point margin, for which other choices were possible. Stratford et al reported that a clinically important RMDQ change varies with initial score: 2 for 0 to 8, 4 for 5 to 12, 5 for 9 to 16, 8 for 13 to 20, and 8 for 17 to 24. Because this trial’s initial score was 14, the authors considered that a higher margin might have been chosen, while noting that a non-inferiority margin cannot be determined solely from an individual patient’s minimum detectable change. They emphasized stratifying patient populations when evaluating meaningful pain scores in future studies.

document_sections.heading: Perioperative Outcomes
document_sections.content: Operative time and blood loss significantly favored PEEK: 127min versus 150min and 317ml versus 473m, respectively, as stated in the discussion. The authors linked greater Si3N4 blood loss directly to longer operations, but noted that one Si3N4 patient with 1700ml blood loss skewed this result. More double-level procedures with Si3N4 than with PEEK, 8 versus 5, could partly explain the operative-time difference. During insertion in 2 patients, rotation fractured a Si3N4 cage at the insertor–cage interface. Replacement prolonged surgery. The authors attributed these fractures to insufficient interface stability; after modifying the insertor tip to improve its grip, no further fractures occurred. Other perioperative complications were distributed across the study period.

document_sections.heading: Radiological Outcomes
document_sections.content: The authors noted continuing disagreement in the literature about when a lumbar segment qualifies as radiologically fused. Proposed criteria combine angular and translational motion, anterior bridging bone, and absence of lucency at implant surfaces. PEEK radiolucency made interface lucency and osseous integration unreliable measures in this trial. The usable measures were CT bridging bone from one endplate to the other at 12 months, disc-height change as an indicator of subsidence, and flexion/extension segmental motion. Neither average subsidence nor bridging bone differed significantly between groups. Motion-based fusion required angular motion < 2 and translational motion < 0.5mm, and the resulting fusion rates resembled published results. The authors cautioned that incomplete technical or radiographic fusion need not mean clinical failure: stability may precede visible fusion, and a clear link between bony fusion and favorable clinical outcome has not been established.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Revisions were more frequent after Si3N4 than after PEEK, 10 vs 4, but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.10). The discussion identifies adjacent-level problems as the leading reason for revision. It also notes that two Si3N4 cages fractured during surgery because of a technical problem at the insertor–cage interface.

document_sections.heading: Limitations
document_sections.content: Using one oblique cage permitted more accurate CT fusion measurements but provided less mechanical stability than 2 parallel cages; the authors considered this a possible source of bias and a possible explanation for the 15.2% revision rate. They also identified the choice of the 2.6-point RMDQ non-inferiority margin as a limitation. Manufacturer funding was another potential source of bias. The authors stated that they sought to reduce it through independent study management, statistical analysis, and radiographic measurement.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: Both groups improved on RMDQ by up to 5-8 points after 24 months, but the evidence remained insufficient to conclude that Si3N4 was non-inferior to PEEK. Surgery took significantly longer and involved significantly more blood loss with Si3N4. Complications and revisions also appeared more frequent with Si3N4, although those differences were not statistically significant.
